items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: And I later played with him, you know, also, and we used to alternate. He'd play tenor some and I'd play alto, because we were both alto players.

ctx.x: But anyway, we stayed out there with that band and I played tenor in that band. That was the St. Louis Merry-makers, that was the name of that band. Now that was like the first band that I worked with after leaving the McCloud's Night Owls. They called the band the St. Louis Merrymakers.

So then Troy Floyd was pretty -- name band then, you know. It was a bigger name than the St. Louis Merrymakers. So a friend of Herschel's had been trying to get him in that band for a long, long time and the tenor player that was playing in the band was a tenor player by the name of Funny Bagsby and he quit the band, Funny Bagsby was his name. I never forget. So Herschel joined that band. They told him they'd let him play tenor and that's when he went to Troy Floyd to play tenor. And I later played with him, you…
And then all the time though, after Milton, I was listening to a tenor player, me and Herschel, also Milton, by the name of Prince Robinson. That's Harold Vick's uncle.

items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: Well I didn’t think Herschel had a bad night, Herschel Evans.

ctx.x: Well I didn’t think Herschel had a bad night, Herschel Evans. I never thought he had a bad night. Of course Lester declined in his later years from health problems though, with Lester, and I never know what put him on the wrong track because for so many years he was just a health bug. And he was very unhappy with himself the last time we were together we played up to Newport Jazz Festival and he was very sick, he was drinking and drinking. And I rode back with him from Newport and we got lost, which Newport is…
no eagle eyes,” he says, “but I never really made any money.” He didn’t make any money that night.
